title: Phase Detectors and the Simple PLL
intro: The phase detector, the basic phase-locked loop built from a PD, a low-pass filter and a VCO, and how it behaves when locked (Razavi, Sections 16.1.1 and 16.1.2).

blocks.text: A phase detector produces an output whose average is proportional to the phase difference between its two inputs. The slope is the PD gain $K_{PD}$, in V/rad:

An XOR gate is the classic example. Its output pulses are as wide as the misalignment between the inputs, on both rising and falling edges. If the output swings $V_0$, each extra radian of phase difference widens two pulses per period, so

independent of frequency. The characteristic is a triangle: it rises to $V_0$ at $\Delta\phi = \pi$ and falls back to zero at $2\pi$, so it has regions of positive and negative gain and zero gain at the peaks.

blocks.alt: A triangular wave: average output rises linearly from zero at zero phase difference to V0 at pi, falls to zero at 2 pi, and repeats; it is symmetric for negative phase.
blocks.caption: XOR phase detector characteristic.

blocks.text: A D flip-flop clocked by one input and sampling the other is a bang-bang phase detector: its average output jumps from $-V_1$ to $+V_1$ as $\Delta\phi$ crosses zero (very high gain there, zero elsewhere). It is not a frequency detector: with unequal input frequencies its average output is zero either way.

blocks.alt: Block diagram of a charge-pump phase-locked loop. The reference frequency enters a phase detector, followed by a charge pump, a loop filter and a voltage-controlled oscillator. The oscillator output is the loop output and also goes through a divide-by-N block back to the second input of the phase detector.
blocks.caption: A charge-pump PLL. The divider brings the VCO frequency down so it can be compared with the reference.

blocks.text: To align a VCO's edges with a reference you must change its frequency temporarily and let the phase accumulate, then return the frequency when the edges line up. A PD in a loop with the VCO does this automatically. The PD output carries both the wanted DC term and large high-frequency components, and the VCO control must stay quiet, so a low-pass filter sits in between.

blocks.alt: Block diagram: Vin enters a phase detector, whose output goes through a low-pass filter to a VCO; the VCO output is the loop output and returns to the second input of the phase detector.
blocks.caption: The simple PLL.

blocks.text: Define lock as a phase difference $\phi_{out} - \phi_{in}$ that does not change with time. Differentiating gives the key property:
In lock at input frequency $\omega_1$, the VCO needs $V_{cont} = (\omega_1 - \omega_0)/K_{VCO}$, and the PD (with a filter of unity DC gain) can only produce it from a phase error:

So the phase error changes with input frequency, and making it small needs a large $K_{PD}K_{VCO}$, often called the loop gain although it has units of 1/s. If the input frequency demands a control voltage the PD can only reach at the peak of its characteristic, where its gain is zero, the loop cannot hold lock.
The small pulses left on the filter output in lock are ripple; they modulate the VCO and produce sidebands.

Phase step at the input: the filter output cannot jump, so the VCO keeps its frequency at first; the growing phase error widens the PD pulses, $V_{cont}$ rises, the VCO speeds up until it has gained exactly the extra phase ($\int \Delta\omega_{out}dt = \phi_1$), and then returns to its original frequency. Afterwards the control voltage, phase error and frequency are all as before.

Frequency step: the VCO must end at the new frequency, so the control voltage and the phase error both change permanently, by $\Delta\omega/K_{VCO}$ and $\Delta\omega/(K_{PD}K_{VCO})$. A slowly varying input frequency is simply tracked.

For the loop to settle, frequency and phase must both settle; a ringing $V_{cont}$ can pass its final value while the phase is still wrong, and vice versa. $V_{cont}$ is the convenient thing to watch in simulation, since phase and frequency are hard to probe directly.

blocks.title: XOR detector
blocks.text: An XOR phase detector swings $V_0 = 1.2\text{ V}$. Find $K_{PD}$ and the average output at $\Delta\phi = \pi/4$.

blocks.title: Locked phase error
blocks.text: A simple PLL has $\omega_0 = 2\pi \times 900\text{ MHz}$, $K_{VCO} = 2\pi \times 100\text{ MHz/V}$, $K_{PD} = 0.5\text{ V/rad}$ and a filter with unity DC gain. It locks to 950 MHz. Find the control voltage and the phase error.

blocks.title: Lock range of an XOR loop
blocks.text: With the XOR detector of the first problem ($V_0 = 1.2$ V, characteristic from 0 to $V_0$ over $0 \le \Delta\phi \le \pi$), a unity-gain filter, and the VCO of the second problem, what input frequencies can the loop hold?
solution: The control voltage can only be between 0 and 1.2 V, so $f_{out}$ ranges over $900$ to $900 + 100 \times 1.2 = 1020\text{ MHz}$.
Near the ends the PD gain falls to zero (phase error near 0 or $\pi$), so in practice the usable range is somewhat narrower.
